'''''Genista tinctoria''''', the '''dyer's greenweed'''<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007|access-date=2014-10-17   }}</ref> or '''dyer's broom''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] Fabaceae. Its other common names include dyer's whin, waxen woad and waxen wood. The Latin [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''tinctoria'' means "used as a dye".<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book | last=Harrison |first=Lorraine | title=RHS Latin for Gardeners | year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley | location=United Kingdom | isbn=978-1845337315 }}</ref>

==Description==
It is a variable [[deciduous]] shrub growing to {{convert|60|-|90|cm}} tall by {{convert|100|cm|0|abbr=on}} wide, the stems woody, slightly hairy, and branched. The alternate, nearly [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] leaves are [[glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]] and [[leaf shape|lanceolate]]. Golden yellow pea-like flowers are borne in erect narrow [[racemes]] from spring to early summer. The fruit is a long, shiny pod shaped like a green bean pod.<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=[[Dorling Kindersley]]|location=[[United Kingdom]]|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
This species is [[native plant|native]] to meadows and pastures in [[Europe]] and [[Turkey]].<ref name=botanical>{{cite web|url= http://botanical.com/botanical/mgmh/b/brodye72.html|title=Broom, Dyer's|access-date=November 30, 2012}}</ref>

==Properties and uses==
Numerous [[cultivar]]s have been selected for garden use, of which 'Royal Gold' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/94064/Genista-tinctoria-Royal-Gold/Details |title=Genista tinctoria 'Royal Gold'|access-date=9 July 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 42 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 27 February 2018}}</ref>

The plant, as its Latin and common names suggest, has been used from ancient times for producing a yellow dye, which combined with [[woad]] also provides a green colour.<ref name=botanical/>

It was from this plant that the [[isoflavone]] [[genistein]] was first isolated in 1899; hence the name of the chemical compound. The medicinal parts are the flowering twigs.

The plant has been used in popular medicine and [[herbalism]] for various complaints, including skin diseases, even in modern times.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Walter ED|year=1941|title=Genistin (an isoflavone glucoside) and its aglucone, genistein, from soybeans|journal=J Am Chem Soc|volume=62|issue=12|pages=3273–3276|doi=10.1021/ja01857a013}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=The Herb Book|author=John Lust |page=176}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Curative Properties of Honey and Bee Venom|author=N. Yoirish|year=2001|page=111|publisher=The Minerva Group |isbn=9780898754094|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JlSJDj5Lt98C&q=%22woad-waxen%22%7C%22Genista+tinctoria%22%7C%22dyer%27s+broom%22+herpes+OR+tetters&pg=PA111}}</ref>
